Q: Interface and Implementation in .Net A:

My recommendations are:

  1. Make your namnespaces match your folder structure. With some few exceptions for special circumstances.
  2. Organize related files into folders to help with organization and navigation as much as possible. In some cases it might be better to put both interfaces and implementations in the same folder. In some cases it can be better to put a bunch of related interfaces in a folder, and one folder per implementation, or one for all implementations. There is no single right answer here.
  3. Try to avoid duplicated type names where practical.
  4. Avoid using the same name as both the namespace and type name.
  5. One type per file. Unless the types are tightly coupled and very small.

Note that with a good IDE the namespaces and folders are not all that important. If you write a class name the IDE should add the namespace automatically, or suggest options in case of ambiguity. And there should be search tools for opening the file for a class, and for navigating to an open file in the solution explorer.

Note that some types of projects have their own conventions. If the template for project type uses some default folders it may be a good idea to stick with that convention for the related types, like a "Controllers" folder for your controllers in a webapi project.

Q: in Vim about netrw: choose differents viewers A:

That option is apparently on its way out because it is undocumented in my version of Vim while still being present as a fallback in Netrw's code. That's not very clean if you ask me.

Regardless, the default behavior of x is to call a system-level utility (xdg-open, open or start, depending on the system) that is responsible for choosing the right "viewer" for the given path. Since that function can't reasonably be fulfilled by a PDF viewer (though anything is possible) it doesn't make much sense to use qpdfview as value, here.

In other words, let x use xdg-open (assuming you are on "Linux") and configure file associations at the system level: qpdfview for PDFs, lximage for images, etc.

Q: Redirecting stdout to "nothing" in python A:

A bit late to the party, and wanted to share a recently discovered method, applicable to Python 3.8+.

Using os.devnull:

The question is how to 'send stdout to nothing'. Well, let's do just that, using /dev/null.

import contextlib
import os

with contextlib.redirect_stdout(f := open(os.devnull, 'w')):
    ... # code continues
    f.close()

The named expression file handle (f) is assigned during the call to open, and thus can be closed at the end of the redirection context. Thanks to the fondly named, 'walrus operator'.

The key that separates this answer from others, is the ability to close the file handle responsibly and prevent the ResourceWarning and underlying file access issues.

Background:

The following method, while more simple, does work in some contexts. However, this had undesired side effects which ultimately resulted in unit tests failing; which lead to the implementation shown above.

with contextlib.redirect_stdout(None):
    ...  # code continues

Q: How should I structure a 50-day learning plan for React and Node.js as a beginner with JavaScript basics? A:

most resources provide long-term roadmaps (3–6 months), which does not fit my timeline.

You could always compress it and take more of the courses in a single day or whatever. These programs may not be designed for full-time study.

But, realistically, learning languages and frameworks like this thoroughly enough that you could build some meaningful real-world software takes time - both to complete the studies and let your brain have time to absorb the concepts, and have time to practice them outside the context of the basic course exercises. This is why you won't really see any programs much shorter than that. You can try and do it in less but be aware that it could be a hard slog.

P.S. You never stop learning as a developer, in any case.
